chapter_summary:
Bringing your game from development to players involves **packaging and deployment**. Packaging is the process of compiling your game's code, assets, and configurations into a standalone executable that can be distributed. Unreal Engine offers several **build configurations**, each serving a different purpose. `DebugGame` includes full debugging symbols and is slowest, ideal for deep debugging. `Development` is optimized for performance but still includes some debugging information and profiling hooks, suitable for internal testing. `Shipping` is the most optimized build, stripping out all debugging information, logging, and editor-specific code, resulting in the smallest and fastest executable, intended for public release. When packaging, you select your target platform (e.g., Windows 64-bit, Mac, Android, iOS) and the desired build configuration. The process can be initiated from the editor via `File -> Package Project -> [Platform]`, or more robustly via command-line tools for automated builds. It's crucial to ensure all necessary plugins are enabled and configured correctly, and that your project settings (e.g., default maps, game instance, packaging settings) are properly set up for your target platform. Common mistakes include packaging with a Development build when a Shipping build is intended, leading to larger file sizes and potential performance issues, or forgetting to include necessary content via packaging settings.

For any serious game development, especially in a team environment, **version control** is non-negotiable. Git is the industry standard, and understanding its basics is paramount. Git tracks changes to your files over time, allowing you to revert to previous versions, collaborate with others, and manage different branches of development. For Unreal Engine projects, a well-configured `.gitignore` file is absolutely critical. Unreal projects generate a vast number of temporary, derived, and binary files that should *not* be committed to your Git repository. These include the `Binaries`, `Build`, `DerivedDataCache`, `Intermediate`, `Saved` folders, and various log files. Committing these large, frequently changing files will bloat your repository, lead to constant merge conflicts, and make collaboration impossible. A good `.gitignore` ensures that only your source code (`.cpp`, `.h`), configuration files (`.ini`), and essential assets (`.uasset`, `.umap`, etc.) are tracked. You can find comprehensive `.gitignore` templates specifically for Unreal Engine projects online, and it's highly recommended to start with one of these.

Once your `.gitignore` is set up, the basic Git workflow involves:
1.  **`git add .`**: Stages all changes in your working directory. You can also stage specific files.
2.  **`git commit -m "Your descriptive message"`**: Records the staged changes to your local repository history. Commit messages should be clear and concise, explaining what changes were made.
3.  **`git push origin <branch-name>`**: Uploads your local commits to the remote repository (e.g., GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket).
4.  **`git pull origin <branch-name>`**: Downloads and integrates changes from the remote repository into your local branch. This should be done frequently, especially before starting new work, to stay synchronized with your team.
For team collaboration, branching strategies become important (e.g., `main` branch for stable releases, `develop` branch for ongoing work, feature branches for individual tasks), but for individual projects, a single `main` branch might suffice. The safety net provided by version control is invaluable; it allows you to experiment freely, knowing you can always revert if something goes wrong, and provides a robust backup of your entire project history. Always commit frequently with small, logical changes, and always pull before pushing to minimize merge conflicts.

screens.title: Packaging, Deployment & Version Control
screens.subtitle: From editor packaging to a clean Git workflow for Unreal Engine projects

narration.text: This chapter brings two essential production skills together: packaging your Unreal project into a distributable build, and keeping your project healthy in Git with a careful. gitignore and basic workflow. You will learn what packaging actually does — compiling code, collecting assets, and producing a platform-specific executable — and why build configurations like DebugGame, Development, and Shipping matter for performance and debugging. You will also see why Unreal projects must exclude generated binaries and caches from source control, and how to use Git commands to stage, commit, push, and pull changes safely. By the end you should be able to package a simple game for Windows, create an effective. gitignore, and perform the core Git operations that every team relies on. As you follow along, notice the practical checks: verify default maps, enable required plugins, and close the editor before repository operations. Think about what would happen if a team committed build artifacts — how would cloning and merging change? That question frames our hands-on activities.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Packaging prepares a playable executable for players; Git protects work and enables collaboration. Together they move a game from a single machine to a team and to players.

screens.title: What is Packaging?
screens.subtitle: Definition and concrete example of how packaging produces a playable build

narration.text: Packaging is the process of converting your in-editor project into a standalone package that players can run. Practically, packaging compiles C++ code, cooks assets into platform-ready formats, gathers configuration such as default maps and game instance, and places everything into a destination folder as an executable and supporting files. For example, packaging a small Windows build will compile your game modules, cook textures and meshes, and produce a folder with an. exe that someone can double-click to play. The important parts to verify are that default maps are set, required plugins are enabled, and that any editor-only content is not expected in the runtime. A common misconception is that packaging just zips assets; it actually runs the compiler and asset cooker so runtime formats and platform-specific binaries are produced. In practice you will choose a build configuration that affects what information is kept: DebugGame keeps debugging symbols, Development balances profiling and speed, and Shipping strips all debugging for the smallest, fastest runtime. Before packaging, always confirm maps and plugin settings and consider running a Development build first to test behavior, then create a Shipping build for release. How will you verify that the packaged executable contains the correct default map and runs as expected?

keyIdea.title: Packaging in one line
keyIdea.text: Packaging compiles code and cooks assets to create a platform-specific executable that players can run.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › What is Packaging?
Definition
Packaging explained
Packaging bundles compiled game modules and cooked assets into a distributable folder. It converts editor content into runtime formats and includes platform-specific binaries so the game runs outside the editor.
Compile C++ modules and link binaries for the target platform.
Cook assets into runtime-friendly formats and include them in the build.
Collect configuration such as default maps, game instance, and packaging settings.
Concrete example
Windows package of a small project
A Windows packaging run compiles modules to a 64-bit executable, cooks textures and maps, and produces a folder with the .exe and content subfolders. Run the executable to verify launch and the chosen default map.
Checklist before packaging
  • Default maps set in project settings.
  • Required plugins enabled and configured.
  • Packaging destination selected and disk space available.
Common mistake
Packaging with Development or DebugGame when Shipping was intended leads to larger files and retained debug hooks. Verify build configuration before long runs.
Key Takeaway

Packaging is more than copying files; it compiles, cooks, and configures a playable build you can test and ship.

screens.title: Build Configurations: DebugGame, Development, Shipping
screens.subtitle: How each configuration affects debugging, size, and performance

narration.text: Build configurations change the compiler flags, what symbols are kept, and which runtime code is included. DebugGame includes extensive debugging symbols and instrumentation so you can step through code and inspect state, but it results in the slowest runtime and largest binaries. Development strikes a balance: it keeps some profiling hooks and lighter debugging information so internal testing is efficient while giving better performance than DebugGame. Shipping removes debugging symbols, logging, and editor-only code, producing the smallest and fastest executable ready for public distribution. A practical example: when a crash happens only on a tester's machine, a Development build can help reproduce and profile the problem; but when releasing to players, Shipping is the correct choice to avoid exposing developer consoles or leaving debugging hooks enabled. A common error is packaging a Shipping build during active debugging — you lose diagnostic signals and stack traces. Another mistake is always testing only in Shipping; subtle bugs can be harder to locate without the extra diagnostics Development provides. To choose properly, ask: am I debugging or releasing? Use Development to test and Shipping to publish. How will you plan packaging runs to include both test and final release builds?

keyIdea.title: Pick the right config
keyIdea.text: Use Development for testing and profiling, DebugGame for deep debugging, and Shipping for final releases to players.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Build Configurations
Comparison
DebugGame vs Development vs Shipping
DebugGame
Full debugging symbols and instrumentation for deep troubleshooting. Slow and large.
When to use: step-through debugging and deep inspection.
Development
Balanced: keeps some diagnostics and profiling hooks while improving performance. Good for internal testing.
When to use: iterative testing and profiling before release.
Shipping
Optimized build with debugging removed. Smallest and fastest; intended for public release.
When to use: final release to players.
Example scenario
If a performance issue appears in QA, build in Development to profile. If the issue remains unclear at that stage, reproduce in DebugGame to step through code. Only produce Shipping builds for distribution.
Pitfall
Shipping removes logs and debug hooks. Avoid shipping when debugging or you will lose diagnostic context.

screens.title: Packaging Steps in the Editor
screens.subtitle: A clear sequence to create a packaged build from the Unreal Editor

narration.text: Packaging from the editor follows a repeatable sequence that reduces mistakes. First, prepare your project: confirm default maps, ensure required plugins are enabled, and set packaging settings such as included directories and compression. Next, choose the build configuration you need for this run: Development for testing or Shipping for final output. Then select the target platform and a destination folder with sufficient space. Start the packaging operation and monitor the log for missing assets or cooking errors. When it completes, navigate to the output folder and run the executable to validate launch, default map, and basic gameplay. A useful practice is to perform a Development run first to catch issues early, then run a Shipping package once everything is verified. Common misconceptions include assuming packaging always succeeds silently — many issues appear only in the log, so review it. Another frequent mistake is not testing the packaged executable; success in the editor does not guarantee the packaged build will run the same. Make a short checklist and follow it each time you package to avoid rework and wasted build time.

keyIdea.title: Repeatable packaging pipeline
keyIdea.text: Prepare, select config and platform, run packaging, review logs, and validate the packaged executable.

screens.title: Command-line and Automated Packaging
screens.subtitle: How to automate builds and why command-line packaging helps CI

narration.text: Automated packaging via command-line tools enables reproducible builds and continuous integration. Instead of manually initiating packaging in the editor, you can call the Unreal build and cook tools or invoke editor commands in a script to select platform, configuration, and output folder. This makes it possible to run nightly builds, generate a Shipping artifact on demand, and avoid human steps that cause inconsistencies. The principal benefit is repeatability: scripts produce the same steps every time, and CI systems can archive artifacts. A concrete example is calling the editor in a headless mode to cook content and build the executable for Windows Shipping; this avoids a user opening the editor UI and missing a configuration. A common misconception is that automated builds are only for large teams; even small projects benefit because automation eliminates manual mistakes and saves time. Before automating, ensure your project settings, default maps, and required plugins are configured in the project file so the script will perform the same run every time. Also verify your CI runner has the required SDKs for target platforms. How would you turn your manual packaging steps into a simple script for repeatable builds?

keyIdea.title: Automate for repeatability
keyIdea.text: Use command-line packaging to create reproducible, scriptable builds suitable for CI and nightly artifacts.

Make packaging scriptable
Write a script that invokes the editor's headless or build tools with explicit platform and configuration arguments. Keep configuration in the project file so CI runs can use the same settings.
Why automate?

# Example headless call (visual only)
# Invoke the editor to run a packaging command for Windows Shipping
"UE4Editor.exe" "YourGame.uproject" -run=Cook -TargetPlatform=WindowsNoEditor -unattended
"UE4Editor-Cmd.exe" "YourGame.uproject" -run=Package -TargetPlatform=WindowsNoEditor -cook -build

Checklist for CI
Ensure runner has required SDKs, set environment variables, and archive resulting artifacts for testers.

screens.title: .gitignore for Unreal Engine
screens.subtitle: Why ignoring generated files is essential and which folders to exclude

narration.text: A. gitignore file tells Git which files to leave untracked. For Unreal Engine projects this is essential because the editor and build system generate large binary files and caches that are not useful in source control. Typical folders to ignore include Binaries, Build, Intermediate, DerivedDataCache, and Saved. These folders contain compiled binaries, temp build artifacts, cached cooked assets, and editor session data. If you commit them, your repository will rapidly grow and cause constant merge conflicts because these files change frequently per machine. A correct. gitignore keeps only source code (. cpp,. h), configuration files (. ini), and essential assets (. uasset,. umap). A common misconception is to commit everything ‘just in case’ — this leads to long clones and slow history operations. Instead, initialize Git at the project root, add a focused. gitignore, then stage and commit only tracked files. As an example, after adding DerivedDataCache to. gitignore, running git status shows those cache files removed from the staging list. This lets teammates clone a lightweight repository and generate artifacts locally. How will you verify your. gitignore excludes the right folders after creating it?

keyIdea.title: Keep the repo small
keyIdea.text: A properly configured .gitignore excludes generated binaries and cache folders so your repository stays lightweight and merge-friendly.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › .gitignore for Unreal
Definition
Which folders to ignore
Ignore generated and per-machine files: Binaries, Build, Intermediate, DerivedDataCache, and Saved. Also exclude IDE files and temporary logs. Track code, configuration, and essential assets only.
Why ignore these folders?
They are large, machine-specific, and change frequently, which would bloat and fragment repository history.
What to keep
Keep source files (.cpp, .h), config (.ini), and essential assets (.uasset, .umap) needed to build and reproduce content.
Minimal example (.gitignore snippet)
# Unreal Engine generated
Binaries/
Build/
DerivedDataCache/
Intermediate/
Saved/
*.log
# IDE files
.vs/
.idea/
Start with a minimal ignore and add project-specific exclusions. After adding .gitignore, re-run git status to confirm excluded files no longer appear.

screens.title: Git Basics: add, commit, push, pull
screens.subtitle: A terminal-first walkthrough of the essential Git commands for Unreal projects

narration.text: Git provides a small set of commands that let you record and share project changes. Start by initializing a repository at the project root. Then add a well-crafted. gitignore so only the right files are staged. The main sequence you will use is git add to stage changes, git commit to record them locally with a clear message, git push to upload commits to a remote, and git pull to bring remote changes into your working branch. A concrete example: after adding a. gitignore, run git add. to stage the remaining tracked files, then git commit -m "Initial commit of Unreal Engine project" to create a history point. Push that commit to the remote to make it available to teammates. Pull regularly, especially before starting new work, to minimize conflicts. A common misconception is that pushing often is optional; frequent, small commits and pushes make merges easier. Another mistake is committing generated files — large binaries will bloat the repo and slow down every collaborator. In team work, use short-lived feature branches and merge frequently into a develop or main branch. Practice these commands on a small test project until they become routine.

keyIdea.title: Small set of powerful commands
keyIdea.text: Use git add, git commit, git push, and git pull frequently. Keep commits small and descriptive and pull before starting new work.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Git Basics
Code Walkthrough
Essential Git commands
Run these commands from your project root where YourGame.uproject is located. Close the editor first to avoid locked files.
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit of Unreal Engine project"
# Later:
git add path/to/changed/file
git commit -m "Describe the change briefly"
git push origin main
git pull origin main
Guidance and common errors
Commit small, logical changes and write descriptive messages. Always run git status before committing to see unstaged files. Pull before starting new work to reduce merge conflicts.
Pitfall
Committing generated binaries dramatically increases repository size and causes frequent conflicts. Use a good .gitignore.
Pro tip
Make small, frequent commits and push often. This creates logical checkpoints and simplifies collaboration.

screens.title: Create and Verify a .gitignore
screens.subtitle: Practical steps to write a .gitignore and confirm it hides unwanted files

narration.text: Creating a. gitignore is straightforward but requires attention to common Unreal folders. Start by closing the editor, then open a text editor in your project root and create a. gitignore file. Add entries for Binaries, Build, Intermediate, DerivedDataCache, and Saved, plus IDE folders like. vs and. idea. Save the file, then run git status to see which files are still untracked. If you previously committed generated files, add the. gitignore and then remove the now-ignored files from the index using git rm --cached on those paths so they stop tracking, then commit the removal. A concrete sequence: create. gitignore, run git add. gitignore, run git rm --cached -r Binaries Intermediate DerivedDataCache Saved, then git commit -m "Add. gitignore and untrack generated files". A common misconception is that adding. gitignore will retroactively remove files from the repository — it does not. You must untrack previously committed files explicitly. Finally, run git status again to verify only intended files remain. This keeps the repository small and avoids passing large binaries through the remote. Create and Verify a .gitignore means after creating .gitignore, untrack any previously committed generated files and confirm with git status to ensure a clean repository.. In practical terms, practical steps to write a .gitignore and confirm it hides unwanted files. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Make .gitignore effective
keyIdea.text: After creating .gitignore, untrack any previously committed generated files and confirm with git status to ensure a clean repository.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Create & Verify .gitignore
Step-by-step
Make .gitignore and untrack files
If generated files were already committed, you must remove them from tracking after adding .gitignore. Otherwise the repo stays large.
# Create .gitignore with Unreal exclusions
# Then run:
git add .gitignore
git rm --cached -r Binaries/ Intermediate/ DerivedDataCache/ Saved/
git commit -m "Add .gitignore and untrack generated files"
# Verify:
git status
Why the cleanup step matters
.gitignore prevents new files from being tracked, but it does not remove files already in history. Untracking prevents those files from continuing to inflate clone sizes and histories.
Key check
After the cleanup commit, cloning the repo on a fresh machine should not pull large Binaries or DerivedDataCache folders.

screens.title: Team Workflows and Branching Strategies
screens.subtitle: Simple branching patterns for small teams and solo projects

narration.text: Branching organizes parallel work and reduces conflicts. For small teams, a straightforward strategy is to keep a stable main branch for releases, a develop branch for integration, and short-lived feature branches for individual tasks. Developers create a feature branch, commit small changes frequently, push the branch, and open a merge request to integrate changes into develop or main after review. For solo projects, a single main branch may suffice, but it's still useful to create short-lived branches for large changes. The advantage of short-lived branches is that merges are easier and conflicts are less likely. A common misconception is that many long-lived branches reduce risk; in fact they increase merge complexity and lead to painful conflict resolution. Always pull the target branch before merging and resolve conflicts locally. Also consider ignoring generated files in all branches to avoid binary conflicts. A concrete example: implement a gameplay tweak on feature/tweak-jump, commit the small change, push, open a merge request, and merge once tests and smoke checks pass. This keeps history clean and traceable. Team Workflows and Branching Strategies means use feature branches for individual tasks, integrate frequently into develop or main, and avoid long-lived branch divergence.. In practical terms, simple branching patterns for small teams and solo projects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Keep branches short-lived
keyIdea.text: Use feature branches for individual tasks, integrate frequently into develop or main, and avoid long-lived branch divergence.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Branching Strategies
Comparison
Simple branching for teams
Main for stable releases. Develop for ongoing integration. Feature branches for individual tasks. Merge frequently to avoid long-lived divergence and large conflicts.
Feature branch example: feature/ai-improve -> small commits -> push -> merge into develop after review.
Solo project: use main plus short-lived branches when you experiment, then merge and delete.
Practical tips
  • Pull before branching and before merging.
  • Keep commits small and focused to simplify code review.
  • Delete feature branches after merging to reduce clutter.
Mistake
Long-lived feature branches diverge and create merge pain. Integrate frequently instead.

screens.title: Activity Walkthrough: Package and Initialize Git
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step guide to package a small project and set up Git with a .gitignore

narration.text: This walkthrough ties the chapter into a hands-on practice. Start with a small Unreal project and confirm you have a default map in project settings so the packaged build has an entry level. Close the editor before Git operations to avoid locked files. In the editor, run a Development packaging pass to catch issues quickly. Monitor the log for cooking errors and missing assets. After verifying the Development package runs, produce a Shipping package for final verification. For source control, navigate to the project root where YourGame. uproject is located and create a. gitignore including Binaries, Build, Intermediate, DerivedDataCache, and Saved. Initialize Git with git init, add the. gitignore, and then run git add. and git commit -m "Initial commit of Unreal Engine project". If you previously committed generated files, untrack them with git rm --cached -r and commit that removal. Finally run git status to ensure only intended files are tracked. This activity reinforces two critical habits: validate packaged builds by running the executable and maintain a clean repository by excluding generated files. What small checklist will you adopt to make these steps routine?

keyIdea.text: Package then verify builds; set up Git with a .gitignore and commit only tracked source and assets for a clean repository.

screens.title: Common Packaging and VCS Mistakes
screens.subtitle: Troubleshoot repository bloat, missing content, and incorrect build configs

narration.text: There are predictable mistakes learners make when packaging and using version control together. The first is committing generated binaries or caches to Git, which rapidly bloats the repository and makes every clone slow. The second is packaging with the wrong build configuration — for example Shipping when still debugging — which removes diagnostics and complicates troubleshooting. Third, missing plugins or default maps in project settings can result in packaged builds that fail at launch or show empty levels. Fourth, not closing the editor before Git operations can leave files locked or partially written, causing git status to show unexpected changes. To troubleshoot, inspect packaging logs for cook errors and missing asset references; for Git, run git status and look at the list of tracked large files. If large files are already in history, consider using repository-cleaning tools or creating a fresh repository with only the desired tracked files. A useful habit is to run git status and review packaging logs immediately after each packaging operation. This reveals issues early and prevents noisy commits or broken builds from propagating to teammates. What diagnostic step will you add to your pre-release checklist?

keyIdea.text: Check packaging logs and git status immediately. Avoid committing generated files and verify build configuration before long packaging runs.
